narrative:
FIRST WARN FORECAST
Thursday, August 27, 2026

First. Accurate. Trusted.

A BEAUTIFUL STRETCH OF WEATHER

If you like cooler mornings, lower humidity, and plenty of sunshine, the next couple of days are going to be hard to complain about.

The cold front that moved through Wednesday has now cleared southeast Missouri, and noticeably cooler and drier air is spreading across the region. High pressure will gradually move from Missouri toward the Great Lakes through Friday, keeping our weather quiet.

Thursday afternoon temperatures will generally reach the lower to middle 80s across central Missouri, the St. Louis metro, southeast Missouri, and southern Illinois. Some clouds will hang around today, particularly east of the Mississippi River, but we should still see plenty of sunshine.

The biggest difference will be the humidity. Dewpoints are dropping behind the front, so even with temperatures in the 80s, it should feel considerably more comfortable outside.

Tonight gets even better.

Under mostly clear skies and light winds, temperatures will fall into the upper 50s and lower 60s across much of the region. Some of our cooler river valleys in east-central and southeast Missouri may even reach the middle 50s.

We could also see some steam fog developing along area rivers late tonight and early Friday morning because of the significant difference between the warm river water and cooler air above it.

FRIDAY LOOKS JUST AS NICE

Friday may be one of the nicest days of the week.

We should see more sunshine with afternoon temperatures a degree or two warmer than Thursday. Highs will generally reach the middle 80s, while humidity remains relatively low.

Friday night will be another cool one, with widespread upper 50s and lower 60s and a few middle 50s possible in the cooler valleys.

This is certainly not fall yet, but Mother Nature is giving us a pretty good free sample.

Then summer comes back.

WARMING UP SATURDAY

High pressure will move farther east Saturday, allowing winds to turn around and begin bringing warmer air back into Missouri and Illinois.

Temperatures should climb into the upper 80s, with a few locations approaching 90 degrees.

Humidity will begin increasing as well, although Saturday should still be relatively manageable compared to what is coming.

By Sunday, the pattern changes considerably.

SUMMER HEAT RETURNS SUNDAY

A strong ridge of high pressure will build into the Mississippi Valley beginning Sunday, and confidence is becoming quite high that another prolonged stretch of summer heat is coming.

Temperatures should climb well into the 90s Sunday and remain there through much of next week.

The atmosphere several thousand feet above us will become exceptionally warm for this time of year, with temperatures reaching above the 95th percentile of climatology. In plain English, we are talking about an unusually warm air mass for late August and early September.

There is even some potential for temperatures to approach 100 degrees in portions of central and east-central Missouri, including the St. Louis metropolitan area, on one or two afternoons next week.

Humidity does not currently look quite as oppressive as some of our previous heat waves. Dewpoints should generally remain in the 60s rather than spending extended periods in the 70s.

That does not mean it will be comfortable.

Heat index values could still climb to around or slightly above 100 degrees, particularly as we move toward the middle of next week.

There is a little more uncertainty across northeast Missouri and west-central Illinois, where a frontal boundary could stall nearby and occasionally bring clouds or thunderstorms. For most of the region, however, confidence is high that significant heat will return.

And unfortunately, this heat may have some staying power.

NORTHERN LIGHTS POSSIBLE TONIGHT

Tonight could also offer us something considerably more interesting than the temperature forecast.

NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center has geomagnetic storm watches in effect as activity from the Sun approaches Earth. A G1 Minor Geomagnetic Storm Watch is in effect for today, with G2 Moderate storm conditions possible Friday into Saturday.

That means there is at least a possibility that the aurora borealis, better known as the Northern Lights, could become visible farther south than normal.

I want to emphasize the word possible.

Forecasting the Northern Lights this far south is tricky. Whether we actually see anything from Missouri or Illinois will depend on exactly how the incoming solar material interacts with Earth's magnetic field. Sometimes these events overperform. Sometimes we get absolutely nothing.

But with mostly clear skies expected tonight, we at least have the weather cooperating.

If aurora activity becomes strong enough, your best chance will be away from city lights with a clear view toward the northern horizon. A phone camera using night mode can sometimes capture colors that are difficult to see with the naked eye.

And tonight, the Northern Lights are not the only reason to look up.

DON'T FORGET THE LUNAR ECLIPSE TONIGHT

We also have a spectacular lunar eclipse tonight.

This is a very deep partial lunar eclipse, with roughly 96 percent of the Moon entering Earth's darkest shadow at maximum eclipse. That means only a tiny portion of the Moon will remain outside the umbra, so visually it may look very close to a total lunar eclipse.

For St. Louis and central Missouri, the penumbral eclipse begins at approximately 8:23 p.m. The partial eclipse begins around 9:33 p.m.

Maximum eclipse occurs at 11:12 p.m. CDT tonight.

At maximum, nearly the entire Moon will be covered by Earth's shadow and much of it may take on a reddish or copper color.

The partial eclipse ends around 12:51 a.m. Friday, with the final penumbral phase ending around 2:01 a.m.

And unlike a solar eclipse, you do not need special glasses. Just walk outside and look up.

With mostly clear skies expected, viewing conditions across much of central Missouri, the St. Louis region, southeast Missouri, and southern Illinois look quite favorable.

A near-total lunar eclipse and the possibility of Northern Lights on the same night?

That is worth staying up a little late for.

THE BOTTOM LINE

Thursday and Friday will bring some beautiful late-August weather. Expect highs in the lower to middle 80s today, middle 80s Friday, lower humidity, and cool nights with temperatures dropping into the upper 50s and lower 60s.

Tonight could be especially interesting for skywatchers. There is a possibility of Northern Lights if geomagnetic activity becomes strong enough, and we have the lunar eclipse with maximum coverage occurring at 11:12 p.m.

Saturday begins our warming trend with highs approaching 90 degrees.

Then summer comes roaring back Sunday.

Temperatures well into the 90s are expected Sunday through much of next week, and there is even some potential for a day or two near 100 degrees across central and east-central Missouri, including the St. Louis area.

So enjoy these next couple of comfortable days.

And tonight, step outside and look toward the sky.

Sometimes the best forecast is not about what is falling from it.

It is about what is happening above it.

First Warn Weather

First Warn Forecast & Severe Weather Outlook Update
11:50 AM CDT | Wednesday, June 17, 2026
First Warn Weather Alert Day
Headlines
Severe thunderstorms remain likely this afternoon and evening across Missouri and Illinois.
Damaging winds up to 85 mph, large hail up to 2.5 inches, and several tornadoes remain possible.
The greatest threat locally remains across eastern and central Missouri and western Illinois, including the St. Louis metro area.
Strong southwest winds will gust between 40 and 50 mph outside of thunderstorms.
Peak severe weather threat for the St. Louis area remains between 6 PM and 9 PM.

A potentially dangerous severe weather outbreak remains on track across portions of Missouri and Illinois this afternoon and evening. There has been little change in the overall forecast since this morning. The Storm Prediction Center continues to highlight much of eastern and central Missouri and western Illinois in an Enhanced Risk (Level 3 of 5) for severe weather, while portions of central Illinois remain under a Moderate Risk (Level 4 of 5) where the highest threat for significant severe weather exists.

An intense cluster of thunderstorms that developed overnight across Iowa produced wind gusts exceeding 90 mph and continues to influence the forecast across Illinois late this morning. The primary outflow boundary currently extends from far northeast Missouri into portions of south-central Illinois. This boundary will likely serve as a focus for severe thunderstorm development later today.

Strong sunshine south of the boundary is allowing temperatures to rapidly climb through the 80s while dew points remain in the upper 60s and lower 70s. Combined with an exceptionally strong wind field aloft, conditions remain favorable for supercells capable of producing all severe weather hazards.

While morning storms may slightly alter where the greatest risk ultimately develops, confidence remains high that numerous severe thunderstorms will develop this afternoon and continue through the evening hours.

Primary Threats

🌪 Several Tornadoes Possible

A few strong tornadoes remain possible.
Greatest tornado threat remains across central Illinois.
Tornadoes remain possible across eastern Missouri and western Illinois, especially near any lingering outflow boundaries.

💨 Destructive Winds Possible

Widespread damaging winds of 60 to 80 mph.
Isolated wind gusts exceeding 85 mph remain possible.
Significant tree damage and widespread power outages could occur.

🧊 Large to Very Large Hail

Large hail remains possible with discrete supercells.
Hailstones up to 2.5 inches in diameter may occur.
Timing Across Missouri and Illinois
1 PM - 3 PM

The first severe thunderstorms are expected to develop across northeast Missouri and portions of west-central Illinois. Areas near Quincy, Kirksville, Palmyra, Hannibal, and surrounding communities should closely monitor conditions.

3 PM - 6 PM

The severe weather threat expands southeast into central Missouri and western Illinois. Columbia, Jefferson City, Mexico, Bowling Green, Troy, and portions of the northern St. Louis metro could see supercells capable of producing tornadoes, very large hail, and destructive winds.

6 PM - 9 PM

This remains the peak severe weather window for the St. Louis metropolitan area and much of eastern Missouri and western Illinois. Storms may become more widespread during this period while maintaining the potential to produce damaging winds, large hail, and tornadoes. Residents from St. Louis and St. Charles to Edwardsville, Belleville, Alton, Farmington, and surrounding communities should be prepared to act quickly if warnings are issued.

9 PM - Midnight

Storms are expected to organize into a line extending from central Missouri into southern Indiana. Damaging straight-line winds become the primary threat as storms shift into southeast Missouri and southern Illinois. Heavy rainfall and localized flooding may also develop overnight.

Local First Warn Outlook

The highest confidence for severe weather today exists across the Enhanced Risk area covering much of eastern and central Missouri, including Columbia, Jefferson City, the St. Louis metro, northeast Missouri, and west-central Illinois.

Farther south, a Slight Risk extends across southern Missouri and southern Illinois, including Rolla, Salem, Farmington, Fredericktown, Marion, and Mount Vernon. Severe thunderstorms remain possible in these areas, but storm coverage and intensity may be somewhat lower than locations farther north.

The lowest severe weather threat remains across the Missouri Bootheel and far southern Illinois near the Kentucky border where a Marginal Risk remains in place. However, isolated severe storms cannot be ruled out.

Missouri Bootheel

Additional Concern: Strong Winds Outside of Storms

Even outside of thunderstorms, strong southwest winds will continue through the afternoon. Sustained winds of 20 to 30 mph with gusts of 40 to 50 mph are expected. Loose outdoor objects should be secured, and travel may become difficult for high-profile vehicles.

Thursday Outlook

The cold front responsible for today's severe weather will gradually move south of the region overnight. Showers and a few thunderstorms may linger into Thursday, especially across southeast Missouri and southwest Illinois. Cooler temperatures in the 70s and lower 80s will provide a welcome break from today's heat and humidity.

Bottom Line

There has been little change in the forecast thinking since this morning. The atmosphere remains primed for severe thunderstorm development this afternoon and evening. While the greatest threat for strong tornadoes remains across central Illinois, all severe weather hazards remain possible across eastern Missouri and western Illinois.

The St. Louis metro remains in the corridor for severe weather between 6 PM and 9 PM, with damaging winds, large hail, and tornadoes all possible. Everyone across the First Warn viewing area should remain weather aware and have multiple ways to receive warnings throughout the day and tonight.
